title: Royalties
summary: The OECD Model gives the residence State of the beneficial owner the sole right to tax royalties. The Commentary spends most of its length on what counts as a royalty: the line between using a right and buying it outright, know-how versus services, software, digital downloads and mixed contracts. These definition points matter for Saudi treaties too, even though most of them let Saudi Arabia tax royalties at a capped rate.
readingNote: Most Saudi treaties follow the UN Model here and allow source taxation of royalties at a capped rate, and many add equipment rentals to the definition. The OECD guidance on paragraph 1 (no source tax) therefore rarely applies as written, but the guidance on what a royalty is (paragraph 2 below) is used to classify payments under either model.

entries.t: Royalties are treated as income from letting out a right. The letting may be part of a business (a publisher licensing a copyright) or wholly separate from any activity (heirs licensing a patent).
Some States deny a deduction for royalties paid to non-residents. Whether that is allowed under a treaty is a non-discrimination question dealt with in Article 24(4), not here.

sections.heading: Paragraph 1: who may tax, and beneficial ownership

entries.t: Royalties are taxable only in the State where the beneficial owner is resident. The only exception is paragraph 3 (royalties connected with a permanent establishment in the source State).

The beneficial owner requirement deals with payments routed through intermediaries. The term is read in its treaty context, not in a narrow trust-law sense. A source State need not give relief just because the direct recipient lives in a treaty State: agents, nominees and conduit companies with very narrow powers over the income are not beneficial owners.

The test: a recipient is not the beneficial owner if its right to use and enjoy the royalties is constrained by a contractual or legal obligation to pass the payment on. The obligation usually appears in the documents but can also be shown by the facts. It must relate to the payment received; ordinary obligations to pay creditors or suppliers do not count.

Being the beneficial owner does not settle entitlement. Article 29 and the Article 1 guidance on improper use of treaties can still deny benefits, including in treaty-shopping cases where the recipient is the beneficial owner.

The treaty meaning is different from the 'beneficial owner' used in anti-money-laundering and transparency rules (the individuals who ultimately control an entity). That other meaning cannot be used for the Convention.
Relief is still available where an agent or nominee, in either State or a third State, sits between the payer and a beneficial owner who is resident in the other Contracting State.

The Article covers only royalties arising in one State and beneficially owned by a resident of the other. Royalties from third States, and royalties attributable to a PE that a resident has in the other State, fall under Article 21. Abuse through PEs in third States is addressed by Article 29(8).
The Model does not say whether the source-State exemption depends on the royalties being taxed in the residence State. States can settle this bilaterally.

BEPS work flagged a pattern: a low-taxed recipient company owned by non-residents that does not distribute its profits. Article 29 deals with the treaty-shopping side. States that want to deny Article 12 benefits for royalties under preferential regimes can use provisions like those in paragraphs 82 to 100 of the Commentary on Article 1.

Royalties cover payments for using, or being entitled to use, literary, artistic and scientific property, the listed industrial property and know-how, whether or not registered. Damages for infringing or copying such rights are also included.
Payments based on how often a right is used, made to someone who neither owns the right nor holds a right to use it, are not royalties.

A payment for the full ownership of a right is not for its 'use', so it is not a royalty. Transfers presented as sales but limited to a period or territory need a case-by-case look under national IP law. Where distinct, specific property is alienated (more likely with geographic than time limits), the payment is generally a business profit (Article 7) or a capital gain (Article 13). Paying in instalments or, for most countries, linking the payment to a contingency does not change that.
'Payment' has a very wide meaning: it covers any fulfilment of the obligation to put funds at the creditor's disposal as the contract or custom requires.
Payments to secure exclusivity, where an owner agrees not to give the information or right to anyone else, fall within the definition.

Earlier versions of the Model (1963 and 1977) counted rentals of industrial, commercial or scientific (ICS) equipment, including containers, as royalties. That wording was later removed so that leasing income is taxed as business profits under Articles 5 and 7.

Typical satellite 'transponder leasing' payments are for transmission capacity, not for property or information in the definition, so they are not royalties. Even in treaties that keep ICS equipment in the definition, they are usually service fees (Article 7) because the customer never gets the equipment itself. A true lease of a whole satellite to an operator could be equipment rental. The same reasoning applies to cable capacity (for example indefeasible rights of use) and pipeline capacity.
Payments between telecom operators under roaming agreements are not royalties, even under treaties that include ICS equipment, because no property, secret process or information is supplied.
Payments for spectrum licences are not royalties, including under treaties covering ICS equipment, because no equipment is used.
Film rentals for cinema or television are royalties, though treaties may agree to treat them as business profits.
Payments made only to obtain exclusive distribution rights for a product or service in a territory are not royalties. They are aimed at increasing sales and fall under Article 7.

Paying someone to develop a design, model or plan that does not yet exist is a payment for services (Article 7), even if the designer keeps the copyright. Paying the owner of existing plans only for the right to reproduce or modify them is a royalty.

Know-how means undisclosed industrial, commercial or scientific information arising from previous experience, with practical use in a business and economic value if disclosed. It does not cover new information produced by performing services for the payer.

Under a know-how contract the grantor shares existing special knowledge for the other party to use on its own account, without taking part in applying it or guaranteeing results. Under a services contract the supplier uses its own skills to do the work, and payments generally fall under Article 7.

Criteria to tell them apart: know-how contracts concern existing information (or information supplied once created) and include confidentiality terms. Service contracts use special skill without transferring it. Supplying know-how usually needs little more than handing over existing material, while services usually involve much greater cost to the supplier, such as staff salaries or subcontractors.

Listed as services, not know-how: after-sales service, warranty work, pure technical assistance, a customer list built for the payer from public information (unlike a confidential list from the supplier's own dealings, which is know-how), an opinion from an engineer, lawyer or accountant, and electronic advice or access to a non-confidential troubleshooting database.

For computer programming information, a payment is for know-how only where it buys the ideas and principles underlying a program (logic, algorithms, programming techniques), supplied under confidentiality and protected as a trade secret.

Mixed contracts (franchising is the example) should be split, using the contract or a reasonable apportionment, with each part taxed under its own rule. If one part is by far the main purpose and the rest is ancillary and largely unimportant, the whole payment follows the main part.

sections.heading: Paragraph 2: computer software and digital products

entries.t: Classifying software payments is difficult and important. The guidance was introduced in 1992 and refined in 2000. Software can be operational or application software, standard or tailor-made, and delivered on media or electronically.

The character of a payment depends on the rights the buyer acquires. Copyright law generally separates the copyright in the program from a copy of the program, and transactions range from selling the whole copyright to selling a restricted product, which is why the boundary with royalties is hard to draw.
A buyer may acquire rights in the copyright itself, partial or complete, or rights in a copy of the program. Occasionally the deal is really a transfer of know-how or a secret formula.

Paying for partial copyright rights is a royalty where the licence allows uses that would otherwise infringe, such as reproducing and distributing the software to the public or modifying and publicly displaying it. Because software does not fit neatly into the literary, artistic or scientific categories, States may amend paragraph 2 to refer to software expressly.

Where the rights acquired are limited to what is needed to operate the program (copying it to a hard drive or memory, or making an archival copy), those copying rights are ignored and the payment is business income under Article 7. The delivery method and any use restrictions do not matter.
Site, enterprise or network licences that allow multiple copies only for the licensee's own use are, in most cases, business profits under Article 7.

Payments for information about the ideas and principles underlying a program (logic, algorithms, techniques) can be royalties as know-how or secret formulas, unlike an ordinary purchase of a program copy.

A distributor that pays to acquire and distribute copies, without the right to reproduce the software, is buying copies rather than exploiting the copyright. This is business profit under Article 7, whether delivery is physical or electronic and even with minor customisation for installation.

Payment for the full ownership of the copyright is not a royalty. Harder cases are exclusive rights for a period or area, extra payments linked to use, and large lump sums. In general, the transfer of distinct and specific property gives business profits or a capital gain rather than royalties, and the form or timing of payment does not change an alienation.
Software sold with hardware, or software rights combined with services, is apportioned as in paragraph 11.6.

The same principles apply to other digital products such as images, sounds and text. The question is what the payment is essentially for. Downloading a digital product for the customer's own use or enjoyment is essentially the acquisition of data, so the payment falls under Article 7 or 13. Any copying needed to download, store and operate the product does not change that.
By contrast, a payment mainly for the right to use the copyright in a downloaded product is a royalty. Example: a publisher paying to reproduce a downloaded copyrighted picture on a book cover.

For performers, the fee for a concert and any simultaneous broadcast falls under Article 17. Royalties the artist receives on record sales, based on the artist's own copyright in the recording, fall under Article 12. If the copyright belongs to the producer or a third party, the payments fall under Article 7 or 17 even when linked to sales.
Payments for working mineral deposits or other natural resources fall under Article 6, not Article 12.

sections.heading: Paragraph 3: royalties connected with a PE

entries.t: This is not a 'force of attraction' rule. The source State may tax royalties without the Article's limits only where they are paid for rights or property forming part of the assets of the recipient's PE there, or otherwise effectively connected with it.

Moving rights into a PE set up only for that purpose in a preferential regime is usually stopped by Article 29 (especially paragraph 8) and the improper-use principles. A place is a PE only if business is carried on there, and recording a right in the PE's books is not enough to make it effectively connected.
A right is effectively connected with a PE if its 'economic' ownership is allocated to the PE under the OECD report on attributing profits to PEs. For insurers, the report's Part IV guidance applies.

sections.heading: Paragraph 4: excessive royalties between related parties

entries.t: Where a special relationship inflates the royalty above the arm's length amount, the Article applies only to the arm's length amount and the excess is taxed under each State's law, subject to the rest of the Convention. The paragraph allows the amount to be adjusted but not recharacterised (for example as equity). Wording changes are suggested for States that want a wider rule.

The excess must result from the special relationship, such as one party controlling the other or both being under common control. The concept also covers family relationships and any community of interests apart from the royalty arrangement itself.

The excess is classified by its actual nature in each case. If the two States would tax the excess under different Articles, they should resolve this through the mutual agreement procedure, and they may add clarifying wording to the paragraph.

membersNote: Paragraphs 27 to 31.7 are members' observations on this Commentary and paragraphs 32 to 49 are their reservations on the Article. Non-OECD economies' positions are in section P(12).
